Suppose the training data carries a primary label $y \in \{1,\dots,C\}$ **and** a
binary tag $s \in \{\mathsf{r}, \mathsf{f}\}$ that is known while fitting but
irrelevant at inference: retain/forget, clean/noisy, real/synthetic,
source/target, poisoned/benign. The usual reflex is to fit one model per value of
$s$ and combine them afterwards. This note argues for the other order, and calls
the result the **2C construction**.

> Fit a single model on the product space $(y, s)$ rather than mixing separate
> models, because joint normalisation turns the attribute into an exploitable
> direction in logit space.

2C came out of a machine-unlearning problem, but nothing in it is about
forgetting. What follows is the general version: a way of extracting a concept
that you already know how to label.

## Where the normalisation happens

This is the whole point, so it is worth going slowly.

**The mixture route.** For each class $y$, treat the two subpopulations as a
mixture of class-conditional densities:

$$
P(x \mid y) \;=\; \bigl(1 - \pi_{\mathsf f}(y)\bigr)\, P_{\mathsf r}(x \mid y)
\;+\; \pi_{\mathsf f}(y)\, P_{\mathsf f}(x \mid y),
$$ {#eq-mixture}

then apply Bayes over $C$ classes. In words: each class is a bag containing both
kinds of points, and the tag lives *inside* the bag. The softmax competition runs
between $C$ cells; whatever structure $s$ carries is averaged away before the
normaliser ever sees it.

**The 2C route.** Promote the pair $(y,s)$ to a label in its own right and fit a
single model on $C \times 2$ cells:

$$
P(y, s \mid x) \;=\;
\frac{\pi(y,s)\, P(x \mid y, s)}
     {\sum_{y'=1}^{C} \sum_{s' \in \{\mathsf r, \mathsf f\}} \pi(y',s')\, P(x \mid y', s')}.
$$ {#eq-2c}

In words: one softmax over $2C$ cells, so the $\mathsf r$ and $\mathsf f$ cells
of *every* class compete with each other directly, not just within their own
class. Class posteriors come back by marginalising, $P(y \mid x) = \sum_s P(y,s
\mid x)$, so nothing is lost at prediction time.

Both routes describe the same data. They do not produce the same object:

> Mixing then normalising is not the same as normalising then mixing.

@eq-mixture mixes on $X \mid y$; @eq-2c mixes on the posterior. That inversion is
what makes the difference readable.

Two consequences follow, and the second is the surprising one.

**$P(s \mid x)$ comes out for free, coupled to the class structure.** No separate
attribute classifier is needed: marginalising the other way, $P(s \mid x) =
\sum_y P(y,s \mid x)$, reads off the same softmax, and it is estimated jointly
with the class geometry rather than beside it.

**The minority subgroup's covariance is implicitly stabilised.** Take LDA as the
proxy family. LDA-2C has $2C$ mean vectors but a **single** pooled covariance
matrix. The explicit mixture, LDA-Mix, needs two — one of which is estimated on
the $\mathsf f$ subset alone, which is usually the small one. The richer
parametrisation is therefore also the cheaper and the better-conditioned; the
extra means cost $O(Cd)$ parameters while the avoided covariance would have cost
$O(d^2)$ estimated on few points.

## The signal, and why it is reusable

Once the $2C$ model is fitted, marginalise twice — over both tags, and within the
$\mathsf r$ block only — and take the log-difference:

$$
\Delta M(x) \;=\; \log P_{\mathsf r}(\cdot \mid x) \;-\; \log P(\cdot \mid x)
\;\in\; \R^{C}.
$$ {#eq-signal}

In words: for each class, how much more (or less) probable that class becomes
when the $\mathsf f$ cells are dropped from the competition. This is a vector in
logit space, and it can be used in two ways:

- **as a logit processor** — add $\eta \cdot \Delta M(x)$ to the output of a
  black-box model, no weight access required;
- **by distillation** — fold the correction back into the parameters when the
  network is available.

The structural point is that the concept is extracted **once**, and only then
applied, at whatever strength $\eta$ one wants. That is not what fine-tuning
does: there, extraction and application are the same optimisation trajectory, and
there is no object left over that can be turned up, turned down, or merely
measured.

## An admissibility test that doubles as a concept detector

Before extracting anything, 2C answers a prior question that people usually
answer by training something and looking at the result:

> Is the attribute $s$ actually encoded in this representation, at the layer where
> the proxy is attached?

The test compares two proxy likelihoods: the concept is exploitable when the full
$2C$ model explains the data better than its $\mathsf r$-only restriction. That
is a single sum over the dataset, with no gradient computation anywhere —
negligible next to one optimisation step.

A negative test is information, not a failure. It says the concept is not
linearly present at that layer, and the correct response is to do nothing, or to
change proxy family or layer — not to push harder. In the Gaussian family this
happens systematically when the subgroup is not separated at first and second
order, and the honest diagnosis is then "there is nothing to extract here", not
"the method missed it".

Where to attach the proxy: an intermediate layer. Early layers have no class
geometry yet; the last ones are redundant with the logits and therefore cannot
expose a difference the logits do not already express.

## What else the tag can be

| $s$ encodes | What $\Delta M$ gives |
|---|---|
| A spurious attribute (background, texture, watermark) | A shortcut-bias correction direction |
| Clean vs. noisy label | Correction for the contribution of mislabelled examples |
| Real vs. synthetic | A measure of the model's reliance on generated data |
| Source vs. target domain | A domain-adaptation signal without retraining |
| Poisoned vs. benign | Backdoor neutralisation |
| Demographic subgroup | Audit: $\|\Delta M\|$ quantifies how much the decision depends on $s$ |

These are directions, not validated results. The last row deserves its own
sentence, though, because it uses the machinery differently: one does not apply
the correction at all, only measure its magnitude. 2C becomes an instrument
rather than an intervention.
